title: August, Appalachian hardwoods

traps.designNote: The buried-root trap named in the confusion set's teaching note. Jack-o'-lanterns fruit from roots and buried wood, so a cluster can rise out of what looks like bare ground, and substrate — one of the four discriminators — quietly reports the chanterelles' value instead of its own. The player reads it correctly; the evidence is what lies. Nothing about the way it grows recovers this, which is the point: the underside and the smell do. The rate is a game number, not a measurement. A third is high enough that a player meets one inside a single foray and low enough that substrate stays worth checking. Nobody has measured how often it actually happens and this file does not claim otherwise.

designNote:
August is not a preference, it is the only month all three members fruit at once: the Appalachian chanterelle runs June to August, the smooth chanterelle June to November, the jack-o'-lantern August to November. The window in which you can actually be confused by all three is one month wide, and a foray in September would be a genuinely different — and smaller — curriculum.

The jack-o'-lantern is weighted slightly heavier than either chanterelle. That is deliberately not an abundance estimate. A player who meets the toxic member rarely learns 'probably a chanterelle' as a prior and starts confirming rather than identifying, which is the reflex this set exists to break. Eight specimens is about ten minutes.

No number in this file has been reviewed by a mycologist. The phenology it gates on has not been reviewed either — it is copied from the species files, which are themselves unreviewed.
